title: Drop the loser, change the winner?
hook: C came last. Take C off the ballot and recount. Could the winner change?

knows: ranking options and adding up points
doesNotKnow: that removing an option nobody ranks first can change who wins a points-based vote

misconception: Dropping a candidate who came last cannot change the winner.
objective: The learner can explain that removing last-placed C flips a Borda vote from B to A although nobody's A-versus-B order changes, because C sitting between B and A on two ballots doubled B's lead there.

claims.text: With 3 ballots A > B > C and 2 ballots B > C > A, and Borda points 2/1/0, the scores are A 6, B 7, C 2: B wins 7–6 and C is last.
claims.source: A: 3×2 + 2×0 = 6; B: 3×1 + 2×2 = 7; C: 3×0 + 2×1 = 2. Computed from the ballots by totals(true) in Demo.tsx (builder re-run in node 2026-10-14 via a transpile-only harness). Matches brief 2, company/domains/briefs/math.discrete.md, Course: NCM. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own count: A 3x2 + 0 = 6, B 3x1 + 2x2 = 7, C 0 + 2x1 = 2; log line 'With C: B wins 7-6 (C 2)'.

claims.text: Without C, recounted with 1 point for 1st and 0 for 2nd, A beats B 3 to 2 on the same voters' rankings.
claims.source: A first on ballots 1–3 (3 points), B first on ballots 4–5 (2 points). totals(false) in Demo.tsx, builder re-run 2026-10-14. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own count without C (1/0): A 3, B 2; log 'Without C: A wins 3-2'.

claims.text: Voters 1–3 put A above B and voters 4–5 put B above A, before and after C is removed; with C on the ballot, C sits between B and A on ballots 4 and 5, so each gives B a 2-point lead over A, and without C every lead is 1.
claims.source: Derivation under c1 (spec company/design/specs/the-loser-flips-the-winner.md, 'Claims this spec adds'): A-minus-B gap per ballot with C [+1, +1, +1, −2, −2], without C [+1, +1, +1, −1, −1]; gapAB in Demo.tsx. B's 2 + 2 = 4 beats A's 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Own gaps A-B per ballot: with C +1, +1, +1, -2, -2 (C between B and A on ballots 4-5), without C +1, +1, +1, -1, -1; B's 4 beats A's 3, then A's 3 beats B's 2.

claims.text: Positional (points) voting such as Borda count can let a last-placed option decide the winner: it can violate independence of irrelevant alternatives.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 23 (voting; positional voting and independence of irrelevant alternatives); J.-C. de Borda (1781), Mémoire sur les élections au scrutin. Attribution: fact-checker confirms (flag carried from the brief). · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Learner sentence 'Points voting like this can let a last-placed option pick the winner' is an existence claim proved by the stage's own example (c1-c3): no voter's A-B order changes, yet the A-B outcome flips when last-placed C is removed, which is a violation of IIA by its definition. E&K ch. 23 and Borda (1781) not opened; not relied on.

claims.text: Borda rule on the stage: 2 points for 1st, 1 for 2nd, 0 for 3rd; with C removed, 1 point for 1st, 0 for 2nd.
claims.source: The lesson's rule (Borda count with n − 1 points for first down to 0 for last among the candidates on the ballot); brief 2 prediction text. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Rule text on stage and ballotPoints(): n-1 points for 1st down to 0 among candidates still running.

recall.question: In a points-based vote, the candidate who finished last drops out and the votes are recounted. Nobody changes their rankings. Can the winner change?
options: Yes: the dropped candidate changed the point gaps between the others
Only if some voters change their minds
recall.why: A candidate ranked between two others widens the points gap between them on that ballot. Remove it and the gaps shrink, so totals can flip even though every voter's order of the remaining candidates is the same.
